entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Gaius Plautius Proculus, consul of the Roman Republic in 358 BCE, holds a pivotal place in the constitutional history of ancient Rome as the first member of the plebeian gens Plautia to achieve the prestigious consular rank. His election marked a significant milestone in the ongoing Struggle of the Orders, demonstrating the tangible impact of the Licinio-Sextian Laws passed in 367 BCE, which mandated that one of the two consuls must be a plebeian. Proculus's ascent symbolized the gradual but decisive integration of the plebeian class into the highest echelons of Roman political power, fundamentally reshaping the aristocratic character of the early Republic.

During his consulship, alongside his patrician colleague Gaius Fabius Ambustus, Proculus engaged in military actions crucial for Roman security. Livy records that Proculus was tasked with campaigning against the Privernates, a Volscian people who had been raiding Roman territory, while Ambustus confronted Velitrae. Although specific details of Proculus's military exploits are scarce, his tenure contributed to the consolidation of Roman control in Latium, a period characterized by frequent conflicts with neighboring Italian tribes. His election itself, however, was arguably his most significant contribution, proving the viability of plebeian leadership in the Republic's highest office.

The precedent set by Gaius Plautius Proculus had profound and lasting consequences for the Roman political landscape. His successful consulship helped to solidify the gains made by the plebeian class, paving the way for numerous other plebeian families, including later members of the gens Plautia, to attain the consulship and other magistracies. This gradual integration fostered a more stable and unified Republic, diffusing internal tensions that had threatened to fracture the state. The era of patrician monopoly on power definitively ended, leading to a more inclusive, albeit still aristocratic, ruling class.
